screens.title: Introduction to the Hyperledger Project and Its Ecosystem
screens.narratorSegment: We begin by situating Hyperledger as a collaborative ecosystem hosted by the Linux Foundation. Hyperledger is not a single blockchain or a cryptocurrency. Instead, it is an umbrella project that brings together modular frameworks, libraries, and tools targeted at enterprise distributed ledger technologies. In this lesson you will learn the mission behind Hyperledger, why neutral stewardship matters to large organizations, and how different projects within the umbrella solve distinct business problems. As you progress, notice how Hyperledger Fabric is presented as the primary focus of our certification — chosen for its modularity, privacy features, and enterprise suitability. You will also meet complementary projects such as Sawtooth for alternative consensus, Indy for identity, Besu as an enterprise Ethereum client, and Burrow for EVM-based permissioned clients. Understanding this ecosystem helps you decide which pieces to combine for real solutions. Think about a case where an organization needs private transactions and strong identity controls; Hyperledger’s modular approach lets you pick the right components. Keep this perspective in mind: Hyperledger is about open collaboration, not a single product. What advantages does a neutral, community-driven project bring to industry adoption?

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Introduction

Introduction to the Hyperledger Project and Its Ecosystem

An open, vendor-neutral umbrella for enterprise-grade distributed ledger frameworks, libraries, and tools.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

This chapter explains Hyperledger’s mission, the Linux Foundation’s stewardship, and the prominent projects you will encounter in enterprise blockchain designs. You will learn to distinguish projects by purpose and understand when to combine them for real solutions.

By the end, you will be able to name core projects, explain why Hyperledger is not a cryptocurrency, and describe Fabric’s role as the certification focus.

Explore Key Topics
Hyperledger Mission
Open-source, industry collaboration to advance enterprise DLT.
Key Projects
Fabric, Sawtooth, Indy, Besu, Burrow — each solves different enterprise needs.
Fabric Focus
Modular, permissioned framework chosen for enterprise privacy and performance.
Ecosystem Snapshot
Hyperledger Fabric
Permissioned framework for private business networks.
Hyperledger Sawtooth
Modular DLT with alternative consensus options.
Hyperledger Indy
Specialized for decentralized identity and verifiable credentials.

screens.narratorSegment: These objectives frame the outcomes you should reach by the end of the chapter. First, you will explain Hyperledger’s mission and goals within the Linux Foundation and why neutral stewardship accelerates enterprise adoption. Second, you will be able to identify Hyperledger as an umbrella project that provides frameworks, tools, and libraries — not a cryptocurrency — and explain why that distinction matters. Third, you will summarize the purpose of several key projects and match each to real use cases, from decentralized identity to enterprise Ethereum clients. Finally, you will describe Hyperledger Fabric’s role and why our course focuses on it, including its modular design, privacy mechanisms, and suitability for consortium networks. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual cue to support retention and a competency milestone to verify understanding. As you review each card, think about a concrete case where a project’s characteristics map directly to a business requirement. That mapping is the skill we want you to master.

screens.title: What is the Hyperledger Project?
screens.narratorSegment: Hyperledger is an open-source umbrella project hosted by the Linux Foundation that focuses on enterprise distributed ledger technologies. Put simply, it organizes a family of frameworks, tools, and libraries designed to solve business problems with DLT. The mission is to foster a neutral, vendor-agnostic community so industry needs drive development rather than a single company’s roadmap. A concrete example: banking, supply chain, and healthcare organizations can collaborate on shared components without relying on a proprietary vendor. A common misconception is to call Hyperledger a single blockchain or to assume it issues a cryptocurrency; both are incorrect. Hyperledger contains multiple independent projects, each with its architecture and use cases. This separation means you can choose a framework that matches your privacy, throughput, or identity needs. Why this matters: neutral stewardship and open governance increase trust among participants, which is essential for consortium networks. Takeaway: treat Hyperledger as a curated toolkit and community rather than a single product. Consider where neutral governance would reduce adoption friction in your organization. What is the Hyperledger Project? means hyperledger is an umbrella for community-driven, enterprise-grade dlt projects maintained under neutral stewardship.. In practical terms, a definition, mission, and why neutral stewardship matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › What is Hyperledger?
Core Concept

What is the Hyperledger Project?

An open, collaborative umbrella for enterprise DLT frameworks and tools, governed under the Linux Foundation.

Mission
Advance cross-industry blockchain technologies through open-source collaboration.
Why neutral stewardship matters
Neutral governance lets diverse organizations contribute, reducing vendor lock-in and increasing trust for consortiums.
Concrete example
A supply chain network can jointly develop adapters and smart contract templates under Hyperledger, sharing maintenance while retaining organizational control of private data.
Analogy & Misconception

Analogy: an open toolbox

Imagine Hyperledger as a curated toolkit where each tool is a separate open-source project. You pick the tool that fits the job and the community helps improve it.

Common misconception

Do not equate Hyperledger with a single chain or cryptocurrency. It organizes multiple projects for different enterprise needs.

Key takeaway

Hyperledger provides neutral, community-driven building blocks for enterprise blockchain solutions.

screens.title: Role of the Linux Foundation
screens.narratorSegment: The Linux Foundation acts as neutral steward for Hyperledger, providing an organizational structure that encourages many companies to collaborate. This stewardship means the foundation hosts governance, legal frameworks, and infrastructure so participants can focus on technology rather than project administration. A concrete example: multiple financial institutions can work together to define common APIs and compliance features without one bank controlling direction. The process of contributing follows common open-source patterns: propose, review, contribute code or documentation, and participate in governance bodies. This open governance ensures transparency in decision-making and aligns development with broad industry needs. A common misconception is that the Linux Foundation directs code choices; instead, it provides the environment and policies that allow the community to make technical decisions. Why that matters: neutral governance reduces adoption friction because organizations trust that no single vendor will change rules unilaterally. Takeaway: open governance is as important as technical design when planning enterprise DLT deployments. In practical terms, neutral stewardship, community governance, and industry participation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Linux Foundation Role
Definition

Role of the Linux Foundation

Neutral stewardship, governance, and shared infrastructure that lower barriers for enterprise collaboration.

Host & Legal Umbrella

Provides legal and administrative structures so contributors can focus on code and design.

Governance

Transparent processes let community members propose and decide technical directions collectively.

Infrastructure

Shared CI, repositories, and communication channels reduce duplication and speed development.

Concrete example

Banks collaborating on common compliance modules can do so under Linux Foundation policies without ceding control to one vendor.

Common misconception

The foundation does not control technical design; it provides the neutral environment and governance model for contributors to make those decisions.

screens.title: Hyperledger is not a cryptocurrency or single blockchain
screens.narratorSegment: A frequent misunderstanding is to call Hyperledger a cryptocurrency or to think it operates like a single public blockchain. Hyperledger does not issue a token and does not represent one chain. Instead, it hosts multiple independent projects that provide frameworks and tools for permissioned and private enterprise networks. For example, a public cryptocurrency chain focuses on permissionless participation and native tokens; Hyperledger projects focus on permissioned participants, privacy controls, and enterprise-grade features. A concrete contrast: public blockchains often optimize for censorship resistance and wide decentralization, while Hyperledger frameworks prioritize controllable membership, pluggable consensus, and confidentiality for transactions between known parties. This distinction affects architecture and governance: token-driven incentives are absent; governance emphasizes consortium agreements and neutral contribution models. Mislabeling Hyperledger as a cryptocurrency can lead teams to the wrong architectural choices, such as planning for public validators when they need permissioned access controls. Takeaway: choose Hyperledger when your design requires controlled membership, data privacy, and enterprise integration rather than public token economics. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Not a Cryptocurrency
Comparison

Hyperledger vs Public Blockchains

Hyperledger
Permissioned frameworks, no native token, focus on privacy, pluggable components, and enterprise integrations.
Public blockchains
Permissionless participation, native tokens, and design choices favoring decentralization and open validation.
Why it matters

Architectural implications

  • • Permissioned networks allow fine-grained access control and private channels for confidential transactions.
  • • No token economics means governance and incentives are driven by agreements and consortium rules.
  • • Pluggable components enable customization to meet performance and compliance requirements.
Misconception

Calling Hyperledger a cryptocurrency can mislead design decisions; architecture should match required privacy and governance models.

screens.title: Hyperledger Fabric overview
screens.narratorSegment: Hyperledger Fabric is a permissioned blockchain framework designed for modularity and enterprise requirements. At its core are components you will use repeatedly: membership services for identity, ordering services that sequence transactions, peers that endorse and commit transactions, and chaincode that implements business logic. Fabric supports private channels so subsets of participants can run confidential transactions, and it allows pluggable consensus mechanisms to match performance needs. A concrete example: a consortium of manufacturers can use channels so proprietary pricing data is shared only among relevant partners while broader provenance data remains visible to the whole network. A common misconception is that blockchain smart contracts must be public to work; in Fabric, chaincode runs within the permissioned environment and access is enforced by membership policies. Understanding these components helps you design networks that balance privacy, performance, and governance. Takeaway: Fabric’s modular architecture is deliberately built so organizations can assemble components to their requirements rather than accept a one-size-fits-all chain. content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Fabric Overview
Architecture

Hyperledger Fabric essentials

Key components you will configure for enterprise networks: identity, ordering, peers, chaincode, and channels.

Identity & Membership
Certificate-based identities define who can participate and what they can do.
Ordering service
Sequences transactions and delivers blocks to peers; consensus is pluggable.
Channels & Privacy
Channels create private ledgers for subsets of members to limit transaction visibility.
Layered panel
Chaincode (smart contracts)
Encapsulates business logic executed by endorsing peers; access controlled by membership policies.
Endorsement & Validation
Peers endorse transaction proposals according to defined policies before ordering and committing.
Concrete example
Manufacturers use channels to protect proprietary pricing while sharing product provenance on a common ledger.
Key takeaway
Fabric’s modular pieces let you tailor privacy, performance, and governance to business requirements.

screens.title: Fabric's modularity and privacy features
screens.narratorSegment: Fabric’s design centers on modularity and privacy. Modularity means components such as consensus, membership, and ledger storage are replaceable. This allows an organization to select an ordering mechanism that fits desired throughput or resilience and to integrate identity providers consistent with enterprise policies. Privacy is provided through channels and private data collections: channels create separate ledgers for defined subsets of participants, and private collections allow confidential data sharing while keeping metadata on the main channel. A concrete example: you could run a high-throughput ordering service for transaction-heavy workflows while using private collections to share contract terms between two partners. A misconception is that privacy features make auditing impossible — they do not. Fabric records sufficient metadata on the common ledger so authorized auditors can verify transaction flows while detailed payloads remain restricted. The practical significance: when designing for regulated industries, Fabric lets you balance confidentiality with verifiability. Takeaway: modularity and privacy are core reasons Fabric suits consortium use cases. Fabric's modularity and privacy features means pluggable components and channel/private data mechanisms let fabric balance confidentiality, auditability, and performance.. In practical terms, how pluggable components and channels support enterprise needs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Modularity & Privacy
Definition

Modularity and privacy in Fabric

Select and swap components to match organizational needs while using channels and collections for confidentiality.

Pluggable consensus
Choose ordering mechanisms that meet throughput and fault-tolerance targets.
Private data collections
Share sensitive payloads with specific peers while keeping proofs on the channel.
Example & Takeaway
Concrete example
A trade finance workflow uses a high-throughput ordering service and private collections to share contract clauses among issuing banks only.
Misconception
Private data does not eliminate auditability; Fabric records verifiable metadata while protecting payloads.
Key takeaway
Fabric lets you tailor privacy and performance without sacrificing governance and verifiability.

screens.title: Hyperledger Sawtooth
screens.narratorSegment: Hyperledger Sawtooth is a modular distributed ledger platform that emphasizes flexible consensus and transaction families. One notable consensus approach associated with Sawtooth is Proof of Elapsed Time, which seeks to provide fair leader selection in large networks while remaining resource-efficient. Sawtooth’s modularity allows developers to define transaction families — sets of rules and data models — that suit specific applications. A concrete example: an IoT network that requires a lightweight consensus and specialized transaction formats could use Sawtooth to develop tailored transaction families for device telemetry. A common misconception is to assume Sawtooth competes directly with Fabric; while both are modular, they are designed for different tradeoffs and network topologies. Sawtooth’s strengths are alternative consensus models and flexible transaction families, making it suitable for networks where those features align with system goals. Takeaway: choose Sawtooth when you need consensus experiments or specialized transaction families that differ from Fabric’s design tradeoffs. Hyperledger Sawtooth means sawtooth offers modular ledger design, transaction families, and alternative consensus like proof of elapsed time for large distributed networks.. Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Sawtooth
Project Spotlight

Hyperledger Sawtooth

Modular DLT platform with flexible consensus choices and transaction family patterns for specialized applications.

Proof of Elapsed Time (PoET)
An approach to leader election designed to be fair and energy-efficient in large distributed networks.
Transaction families
Encapsulate rules and state models for specific domains, enabling specialized business logic.
Concrete example
IoT deployments that need lightweight consensus and custom transaction formats can use Sawtooth’s families to structure data and validation rules.
Misconception
Sawtooth is not necessarily a drop-in replacement for Fabric; choose based on consensus and domain-specific transaction needs.
Key takeaway
Sawtooth is a strong fit when alternative consensus models and transaction-family patterns align with application requirements.

screens.title: Hyperledger Indy: decentralized identity
screens.narratorSegment: Hyperledger Indy focuses on decentralized identity. It provides reusable components, libraries, and tools to create and manage self-sovereign digital identities and verifiable credentials. screens.title: Hyperledger Besu and Burrow
screens.narratorSegment: Hyperledger Besu and Burrow bring Ethereum compatibility to enterprise environments in different ways. Besu is a full-featured Ethereum client written in Java that supports public and private networks and multiple consensus algorithms suitable for enterprise setups. Burrow is a permissioned blockchain client that includes an EVM interpreter for deploying smart contracts in environments that need high throughput and permission checks. A concrete example: a financial institution wanting Ethereum smart contract compatibility in a permissioned network could use Besu for compatibility with public tooling or Burrow when a lightweight, permissioned EVM execution environment is preferred. A common misconception is that EVM-based clients are only for public chains; both Besu and Burrow demonstrate how EVM semantics can be used within private, governed networks. Choosing between them depends on performance needs, language ecosystems, and whether you need a full public-client feature set or a focused permissioned EVM client. Takeaway: use Besu or Burrow when Ethereum tooling compatibility and EVM semantics are required in enterprise contexts. fullNarratorScript:
We begin by situating Hyperledger as a collaborative ecosystem hosted by the Linux Foundation. Hyperledger is not a single blockchain or a cryptocurrency. Instead, it is an umbrella project that brings together modular frameworks, libraries, and tools targeted at enterprise distributed ledger technologies. In this lesson you will learn the mission behind Hyperledger, why neutral stewardship matters to large organizations, and how different projects within the umbrella solve distinct business problems. As you progress, notice how Hyperledger Fabric is presented as the primary focus of our certification — chosen for its modularity, privacy features, and enterprise suitability. You will also meet complementary projects such as Sawtooth for alternative consensus, Indy for identity, Besu as an enterprise Ethereum client, and Burrow for EVM-based permissioned clients. Understanding this ecosystem helps you decide which pieces to combine for real solutions. Think about a case where an organization needs private transactions and strong identity controls; Hyperledger’s modular approach lets you pick the right components. Keep this perspective in mind: Hyperledger is about open collaboration, not a single product. What advantages does a neutral, community-driven project bring to industry adoption?

These objectives frame the outcomes you should reach by the end of the chapter. First, you will explain Hyperledger’s mission and goals within the Linux Foundation and why neutral stewardship accelerates enterprise adoption. Second, you will be able to identify Hyperledger as an umbrella project that provides frameworks, tools, and libraries — not a cryptocurrency — and explain why that distinction matters. Third, you will summarize the purpose of several key projects and match each to real use cases, from decentralized identity to enterprise Ethereum clients. Finally, you will describe Hyperledger Fabric’s role and why our course focuses on it, including its modular design, privacy mechanisms, and suitability for consortium networks. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual cue to support retention and a competency milestone to verify understanding. As you review each card, think about a concrete case where a project’s characteristics map directly to a business requirement. That mapping is the skill we want you to master.

In addition to conceptual knowledge, you will develop practical skills and a verification habit. You should be able to review project documentation and decide which Hyperledger project fits a given requirement, summarize that choice in a short paragraph, and explain any tradeoffs. You will also practice mapping Fabric’s features — private channels, pluggable consensus, identity management — to real business requirements. A useful activity is to explore the Hyperledger projects page, pick two projects other than Fabric, and write three to four sentences describing their purpose and a matching use case. That exercise tests both recall and applied reasoning. Finally, reflect on governance: explain how open governance shapes development priorities, and how community-driven contributions increase resilience and adoption. Each objective has a verification milestone to help you track readiness for assessments and labs.

Hyperledger is an open-source umbrella project hosted by the Linux Foundation that focuses on enterprise distributed ledger technologies. Put simply, it organizes a family of frameworks, tools, and libraries designed to solve business problems with DLT. The mission is to foster a neutral, vendor-agnostic community so industry needs drive development rather than a single company’s roadmap. A concrete example: banking, supply chain, and healthcare organizations can collaborate on shared components without relying on a proprietary vendor. A common misconception is to call Hyperledger a single blockchain or to assume it issues a cryptocurrency; both are incorrect. Hyperledger contains multiple independent projects, each with its architecture and use cases. This separation means you can choose a framework that matches your privacy, throughput, or identity needs. Why this matters: neutral stewardship and open governance increase trust among participants, which is essential for consortium networks. Takeaway: treat Hyperledger as a curated toolkit and community rather than a single product. Consider where neutral governance would reduce adoption friction in your organization. The Linux Foundation acts as neutral steward for Hyperledger, providing an organizational structure that encourages many companies to collaborate. This stewardship means the foundation hosts governance, legal frameworks, and infrastructure so participants can focus on technology rather than project administration. A concrete example: multiple financial institutions can work together to define common APIs and compliance features without one bank controlling direction. The process of contributing follows common open-source patterns: propose, review, contribute code or documentation, and participate in governance bodies. This open governance ensures transparency in decision-making and aligns development with broad industry needs. A common misconception is that the Linux Foundation directs code choices; instead, it provides the environment and policies that allow the community to make technical decisions. Why that matters: neutral governance reduces adoption friction because organizations trust that no single vendor will change rules unilaterally. Takeaway: open governance is as important as technical design when planning enterprise DLT deployments. A frequent misunderstanding is to call Hyperledger a cryptocurrency or to think it operates like a single public blockchain. Hyperledger does not issue a token and does not represent one chain. Instead, it hosts multiple independent projects that provide frameworks and tools for permissioned and private enterprise networks. For example, a public cryptocurrency chain focuses on permissionless participation and native tokens; Hyperledger projects focus on permissioned participants, privacy controls, and enterprise-grade features. A concrete contrast: public blockchains often optimize for censorship resistance and wide decentralization, while Hyperledger frameworks prioritize controllable membership, pluggable consensus, and confidentiality for transactions between known parties. This distinction affects architecture and governance: token-driven incentives are absent; governance emphasizes consortium agreements and neutral contribution models. Mislabeling Hyperledger as a cryptocurrency can lead teams to the wrong architectural choices, such as planning for public validators when they need permissioned access controls. Takeaway: choose Hyperledger when your design requires controlled membership, data privacy, and enterprise integration rather than public token economics. Hyperledger Fabric is a permissioned blockchain framework designed for modularity and enterprise requirements. At its core are components you will use repeatedly: membership services for identity, ordering services that sequence transactions, peers that endorse and commit transactions, and chaincode that implements business logic. Fabric supports private channels so subsets of participants can run confidential transactions, and it allows pluggable consensus mechanisms to match performance needs. A concrete example: a consortium of manufacturers can use channels so proprietary pricing data is shared only among relevant partners while broader provenance data remains visible to the whole network. A common misconception is that blockchain smart contracts must be public to work; in Fabric, chaincode runs within the permissioned environment and access is enforced by membership policies. Understanding these components helps you design networks that balance privacy, performance, and governance. Takeaway: Fabric’s modular architecture is deliberately built so organizations can assemble components to their requirements rather than accept a one-size-fits-all chain. Fabric’s design centers on modularity and privacy. Modularity means components such as consensus, membership, and ledger storage are replaceable. This allows an organization to select an ordering mechanism that fits desired throughput or resilience and to integrate identity providers consistent with enterprise policies. Privacy is provided through channels and private data collections: channels create separate ledgers for defined subsets of participants, and private collections allow confidential data sharing while keeping metadata on the main channel. A concrete example: you could run a high-throughput ordering service for transaction-heavy workflows while using private collections to share contract terms between two partners. A misconception is that privacy features make auditing impossible — they do not. Fabric records sufficient metadata on the common ledger so authorized auditors can verify transaction flows while detailed payloads remain restricted. The practical significance: when designing for regulated industries, Fabric lets you balance confidentiality with verifiability.
